h1: Rolling out a brewery rebrand: timeline, launch and who to tell first
title: Rolling Out a Brewery Rebrand | Craft Beer School
desc: Plan a brewery rebrand launch: big bang or staged, who to tell first, how to find your chokepoint and how to set a date that holds.
teaser: The new logo is approved. Now the hard part: getting it onto cans, taps and phones without chaos.
standfirst: A rebrand is only finished when drinkers see it. Here is how to announce it, who hears first, how to set a launch date you can keep and how to budget for the roll-out.
sections: A rebrand is finished only when drinkers see it

Six months on strategy and design. Three weeks on the launch. New cans on the loading dock before the floor staff know the story. The distributor hears about it from a retailer. The old logo hangs on in the Google listing for another year.

We see this pattern more often than any other in brewery rebrands. It is avoidable if four things are settled early: how you will announce the change, who hears first, what will hold you up and when the campaign starts. This is the final stage of our guide to rebranding a brewery, written for a brewery selling in India.
Choose big bang or staged before you choose a date

A big-bang launch changes everything on one day, often tied to an anniversary or a festival. It makes noise and gives the local press a date to write about. It also needs every can, sign, tap handle and profile picture ready at once.

A staged roll-out spreads the change over 8 to 12 weeks: taproom first, then packaging, then the formal announcement. It suits a brewpub in Bengaluru or Pune where the taproom does most of the selling and packaged beer comes later. The cost is a stretch where old and new looks sit side by side on the same bar, so keep that window as short as you can.

Write down which one fits and why. Note any fixed dates that drive the plan, such as entering a new state or a fifth anniversary.
Your own staff hear it a week before anyone else

Order matters. Staff come first because they will be asked about it on the first night. Then distributors, then your key on-trade and off-trade accounts, then retailers. We brief the team at least seven days before anyone outside hears a word. Distributors need enough notice to plan how they sell through stock with the old label.

Then list every channel that changes on launch day. For most Indian breweries that is Instagram, Facebook, the WhatsApp Business profile and catalogue, the Google Business listing, the food delivery listings, LinkedIn and the website. Seven profiles means seven logins. Find every one of them the week before, not on the morning itself.
The slowest task sets the launch date

Our rule is simple. Find the single task with the longest and least certain timeline. It is nearly always new packaging. Estimate when it will be done, add one month for surprises and that is your launch date.

In India the slowest task is often the label approval. A changed label usually needs fresh approval from the excise department in each state where you sell. The new label still has to meet FSSAI labelling rules. Rules and timelines vary by state and change, so check the current notification or ask a licensing consultant before you promise anyone a date. Our guide to beer label rules in India covers what has to go on the label.

Old stock is the other drag. Printed cans come in minimum runs. If you hold 20,000 printed 330 ml cans and fill 2,500 a week, that is eight weeks of old cans to use up before the new design can appear. Put that on the plan too.
Start the campaign two months before launch

Count back two months from launch day and start the campaign there. Say approvals and new cans look likely by the end of February. Add a month and you launch at the end of March. Count back two months and campaign planning starts at the end of January.

Those eight weeks hold the teasers, staff training, trade briefings and the launch event. Direct advertising of alcohol is restricted in India, so plan any promotion around the brewery, the food and the story rather than the drink. Plan the event so guests who do not drink have plenty to enjoy as well.
The roll-out costs more than the design

Budget 5 to 15% of a year's revenue for a full rebrand, less for a refresh. Take a brewpub turning over ₹20 lakh a month. That is ₹2.4 crore a year, so 5% is ₹12 lakh and 15% is ₹36 lakh. Put your own revenue into the same sum.

Most owners mentally spend that money on the designer. Much of it goes on the roll-out instead: signage, tap handles, glassware, staff T-shirts, merchandise and the labels you write off. Price each of those as its own line before you agree a design fee.
Put every task on one Gantt chart

A Gantt chart is a spreadsheet with weeks across the top and tasks down the side, each shown as a bar. For a typical brewery rebrand we expect 16 to 20 weeks with rows like these:

  • Final design sign-off
  • Label submissions, one row per state
  • Can and bottle printing
  • Old stock sell-through
  • Taproom signage and tap handles
  • Merchandise
  • Website and social profiles
  • Staff training
  • Campaign and launch event

Your first step this week: build that sheet, colour the slowest row red and work the launch date out from it. If the date makes you nervous, the plan is doing its job. A second pair of eyes from someone who has run launches before will usually spot the row you forgot.
Ankur Napa is a Master Brewer who also works in data and AI. Chatty Girija spent more than 30 years in advertising, hosts the Cheers Chatty Beer Podcast and teaches at Craft Beer School.
faqs: How do you pick a launch date for a rebrand?
Find the slowest task, usually new packaging or label approval, estimate its finish date and add one month. That is the launch date.
When should a rebrand campaign start?
About two months before the launch date. That leaves time for teasers, staff training and trade briefings.
Who should hear about a brewery rebrand first?
Your own staff, then distributors, key on-trade and off-trade accounts and retailers, all before any public announcement.
Do new beer labels need approval in India?
Usually yes. A changed label typically needs fresh approval from the excise department in each state where it is sold. Rules vary, so check the current notification or ask a licensing consultant.
